title: 8.2 Cognitive Biases
summary: Human beings do not make decisions like perfect machines.
bodyHtml:
8.2 Cognitive Biases

Why This Matters

Human beings do not make decisions like perfect machines.

We use shortcuts.

Those shortcuts can be helpful in normal life, but in trading they can create repeated mistakes that feel reasonable in the moment.

These mistakes are often called cognitive biases.

A bias does not mean someone is stupid. It means the mind is leaning in a predictable direction.

If you can recognize the lean, you have a better chance of protecting the trade plan.

What You Should Understand After This Lesson

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • explain what a cognitive bias is in plain language;
  • identify four common biases that affect traders;
  • use simple review habits to reduce one-sided decisions.

Four Common Biases

Bias Plain-language meaning Trading example Simple defense
Confirmation bias Looking mainly for evidence that supports your current idea Staying bullish on EUR/USD or gold while ignoring clear warning signs Ask what evidence would make the trade weaker
Recency bias Giving too much weight to the most recent result Oversizing after a short Nasdaq winning streak or freezing after one bad oil day Review a larger sample of trades
Overconfidence Believing you understand more than you really do Taking larger risk in an index or Brent trade because recent success feels like proof of skill Keep size tied to rules, not mood
Sunk cost fallacy Staying with a bad decision because you already spent time or money on it Refusing to exit a weak gold or oil idea because you waited so long for it Judge the trade by current evidence, not past effort

(Table alt-text: A four-row table defining confirmation bias, recency bias, overconfidence, and sunk cost fallacy, with one trading example and one simple defense for each.)

Confirmation Bias in Plain Language

This bias says:

I already have an opinion, so I only want evidence that agrees with it

A trader with confirmation bias may:

  • highlight only bullish signals on a long idea;
  • ignore a weak market structure change;
  • dismiss any evidence that challenges the plan.

That makes the trade feel more certain than it really is.

Recency Bias in Plain Language

This bias says:

what just happened must be the most important thing

A trader may:

  • feel unstoppable after three wins;
  • feel broken after one sharp loss;
  • treat a small recent sample as if it proves the future.

The problem is not that recent results matter a little. The problem is when they matter too much.

Overconfidence and Sunk Cost

Overconfidence can make traders act bigger than their evidence deserves.

Examples:

  • adding size too quickly;
  • trading too often;
  • thinking rules are no longer necessary.

Sunk cost fallacy appears when a trader keeps defending a weak idea because so much time, effort, or money is already tied to it.

Examples:

  • staying in a weak trade because you spent hours planning it;
  • refusing to admit the setup is gone because you waited all day.

A Simple Bias Defense Routine

Before entry, ask:

  1. What evidence supports this trade?
  2. What evidence weakens this trade?
  3. Am I reacting to a recent win or loss?
  4. Am I confident because the evidence is good, or because my ego feels strong today?

That short routine does not remove bias. It makes bias easier to catch.

One Simple Example

Imagine a trader has three winning trades in a row in a stock-index product.

The next morning, the trader feels:

I am seeing the market perfectly right now

That feeling can create two problems at once:

  • recency bias because the recent wins feel more important than they are;
  • overconfidence because success is starting to feel like certainty.

If the trader then jumps into a gold breakout or a Brent crude setup and ignores warning signs that weaken the idea, confirmation bias joins the problem.

This is how a small mental shortcut can grow into a large trading mistake.

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1: Thinking Bias Only Happens to Other People

Bias is a human issue, not a beginner-only issue.

Mistake 2: Calling Confidence the Same Thing as Evidence

Strong feelings are not the same as strong reasons.

Mistake 3: Reviewing Too Small a Sample

One or two trades rarely tell the full story.

Mistake 4: Refusing to Write Down Counter-Evidence

If you never record what weakens the idea, confirmation bias gets stronger.

use simple review habits to reduce one-sided thinking.
